newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu placates rebellious ally.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu placates rebellious ally.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu patched up differences with a key political ally on Monday ahead of parliamentary votes of no-confidence over the way he runs his government.

The Yisrael ba-Aliya party of Russian immigrants, which had sought more government aid for its constituents, said it had signed an agreement with the chairman of Netanyahu's ruling coalition "on the issue of the demands of the faction".
Netanyahu attached a letter to the agreement in which he stated "he will act according to the arrangements" agreed in the pact.

The statement gave no further details but Army Radio said the government had promised Yisrael ba-Aliya, which is led by Industry and Trade Minister Natan Sharansky, a former Soviet Jewish dissident, more funds for immigrant-related projects.
The agreement appeared to seal the support of the party's seven-member faction in no-confidence motions which opposition parties planned to present in the Knesset on Tuesday.
By all accounts Netanyahu will survive the votes in the 120-seat parliament.

Under Israeli law, the support of at least 61 legislators is required to bring down a government and prime minister -- a number which even Ehud Barak, leader of the main opposition Labour party, said Netanyahu's opponents cannot yet muster.
It remained to be seen however how many of the coalition members who make up Netanyahu's 66-54 majority would embarrass him and abstain as an expression of their disaffection.

Israel's Channel Two television predicted before the Yisrael ba-Aliyah pact that 52 lawmakers would vote against Netanyahu and only 46 would support him. It said the remaining 22 coalition lawmakers would abstain or absent themselves.

A little more than a year into office, the 47-year-old prime minister has come under pressure from coalition members demanding help for constituents and control of ministries he was due to dish out in a cabinet reshuffle.

"Regrettably, we are talking about a huge number of personal and selfish interests," said Michael Eitan, the member of parliament from Netanyahu's rightist Likud party who acts as chief of the coalition faction.
Speaking to reporters, Netanyahu voiced confidence his opponents would fall short of the 61 votes required to force new elections.
"We have a government which will continue. The coalition is stable. There are problems -- they'll be solved," he said.
Netanyahu's spokesman said the Israeli leader still intended to put his new ministerial appointments to votes in cabinet and parliament also on Tuesday.
Ex-general Ariel Sharon was frontrunner for the senior job of finance minister vacated by Netanyahu's Likud party rival Dan Meridor last week in a power struggle over the economy.
Two of Netanyahu's cabinet ministers have quit. Two other ministers boycotted a cabinet meeting on Friday.

Netanyahu's judgement has come into question on issues ranging from Jewish settlement expansion which has plunged Middle East peacemaking into crisis to a political appointment which nearly got him indicted earlier this year.
Israeli political analysts cite Netanyahu's inexperience and massive ambition as possible explanations.
